entries.principle: A modular type scale gives consistency; no ratio has evidence behind it
entries.claim: A modular scale sets every text size as base size × ratio^n, where n is a whole number (for example 16 px × 1.25^2 = 25 px). The scale limits the number of sizes and keeps the steps between them proportional. No controlled study found in this research shows that a geometric scale, or any one ratio, improves reading, hierarchy or appeal ratings. The support is practitioner argument.
entries.mechanism: The formula is size_n = base × ratio^n. The usual ratios borrow their names from musical intervals, because each number is the frequency ratio of that interval: minor second 1.067, major second 1.125, minor third 1.2 (6 to 5), major third 1.25 (5 to 4), perfect fourth 1.333 (4 to 3), augmented fourth 1.414, perfect fifth 1.5 (3 to 2), golden ratio 1.618. A plausible reason for a geometric scale is Weber's law (see type-size-step-jnd): people judge size differences by ratio, so equal ratios give steps that look equally large. That reason is an inference; nobody has tested it on type scales. The traditional print scale (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24, 30, 36, 48, 60, 72 points) is not one fixed ratio: it roughly doubles every five steps, which is a ratio of the fifth root of two, about 1.149, per step.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — no study measured it; fewer distinct sizes plausibly make levels easier to tell apart
effects.satisfaction: unknown — no study found

designMoves: Pick one base size and one ratio and derive every text size from them. Worked values from a 16 px base: ratio 1.2 gives 13.33, 16, 19.2, 23.04, 27.65, 33.18; ratio 1.25 gives 12.8, 16, 20, 25, 31.25, 39.06; ratio 1.333 gives 12, 16, 21.33, 28.43, 37.9, 50.52.

Choose a smaller ratio (1.125 to 1.2) where many levels must fit in little room (phones, dense apps) and a larger one (1.25 to 1.5) where few levels need strong contrast (a marketing page). This is convention, not evidence.
Round to whole pixels only after computing, and keep the rounded set fixed in the tokens.
antiPatterns: Choosing a ratio because of its name or its link to music or the golden ratio.
A scale so fine (ratio under about 1.1) that neighbouring sizes look like mistakes.
Sizes added by hand between scale steps until the scale no longer limits anything.

howToCheck.machine: Collect the distinct computed font sizes s. With the declared base b and ratio r, compute n = ln(s / b) / ln(r) for each size. Pass when every n lies within 0.15 of a whole number (the tolerance allows rounding to whole pixels). Also report the count of distinct sizes and compare it with the Catalog cap. The research gives no evidence-based range for r or for the count; the Catalog sets both.
howToCheck.human: Look at two neighbouring levels side by side and ask whether each reads as a deliberate level.

evidence.strengthNote: Practitioner sources only. The search summary of Tim Brown's 2011 article reported that it defines a modular scale and argues that the base and ratio should be meaningful to the project; its own examples use 1.618. The summary reported no test of any ratio, and a dedicated search found no experiment on type-scale ratios. The classic print scale and the 'doubles every five steps' reading come from a search summary of Spencer Mortensen's essay; the per-step value 1.149 is arithmetic done here. Bringhurst is cited from memory. The interval names and ratios are standard music theory, recalled from memory.

sources.citation: Brown, T. (2011). More Meaningful Typography. A List Apart.
Mortensen, S. The typographic scale (essay on the classic print scale as a scale that doubles every five sizes).
Bringhurst, R. (2012). The Elements of Typographic Style (4th ed.). Hartley & Marks.

entries.caveats: A scale fixes sizes, not hierarchy: weight, colour, case and spacing also signal level, and two levels can share a size. Fluid type (sizes that grow with the viewport) breaks a strict whole-number fit between breakpoints; check the scale at each end of the range. The existing record folklore-golden-ratio already says that any consistent ratio gives order; this record adds the formula, the worked values and the check.

entries.principle: The smallest useful step between two sizes: Weber's law and Stevens' power law
entries.claim: People notice a difference in size by its ratio, not by its amount in pixels (Weber's law). In laboratory tasks the smallest ratio that people detect ranges from about 1% to about 14%, depending on the task. Two text sizes less than about 10% apart therefore risk looking like one size set carelessly. Perceived length grows in step with real length, but perceived area grows more slowly than real area (Stevens' power law), so a shape must gain much more than double the area to look twice as big.
entries.mechanism: Weber's law: the just-noticeable difference (the smallest change that a person detects reliably) is a constant fraction k of the starting value, so delta S = k × S. For visual length and size, sources give k = 0.01 (a textbook example: 100 mm against 101 mm), about 0.03 (a figure one paper calls commonly agreed), 0.06 (a model of visual size judgment) and 0.07 to 0.14 (circle sizes at 84% correct). These are best-case values: the two items sit side by side and the person is asked to compare them. On a page, the two sizes are apart and nobody is asked, so the useful step must be several times the threshold. Stevens' power law: perceived magnitude = constant × (physical magnitude)^a. The exponent a is about 1.0 for the length of a line and about 0.7 to 0.8 for area. Text height behaves like length. A block or icon behaves like area: doubling its area makes it look about 2^0.7 = 1.62 times as big.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — levels that differ clearly can be told apart without comparing them side by side; this is an inference from the psychophysics, not a measured result on text
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Keep neighbouring text sizes at least about 12% apart (a ratio of 1.125 or more), or separate them with weight, colour or case as well.
Where two sizes differ by under 10%, merge them into one.
To make a block, badge or icon look twice as big, give it about 2.4 to 2.7 times the area (2^(1/0.8) to 2^(1/0.7)), which is about 1.55 to 1.64 times the width and height.
Think in ratios: 14 px to 16 px is the same visual step as 28 px to 32 px.
antiPatterns: Text sizes of 15 px and 16 px used as two levels.
Adding a fixed 2 px per level at large sizes, where 2 px is a tiny ratio.
Doubling the area of a 'featured' card and expecting it to look twice as important.

howToCheck.machine: Sort the distinct computed font sizes and compute each neighbouring ratio r = larger / smaller. Flag r < 1.10 unless the two text styles also differ in font weight, colour or letter case. Report r between 1.10 and 1.125 as a warning. For paired elements meant to show emphasis by size, report the area ratio A2 / A1 and the predicted perceived ratio (A2 / A1)^0.7. The 1.10 and 1.125 limits are an inference from laboratory thresholds; no study gives a threshold for text hierarchy, so the Catalog owns the number.
howToCheck.human: Show two neighbouring levels apart from each other, not adjacent, and ask a person which is larger. A hesitation means the step is too small.

evidence.strengthNote: Weber's law and Stevens' power law are long-established psychophysics, but every figure here comes from a search summary, and the figures disagree with each other because the tasks differ. The 1/100 figure is a textbook example. The 0.07 to 0.14 range is attributed to Solomon, Morgan and Chubb (2011); the task details were not read. The 'about 3%' figure was reported second-hand. The exponents 1.0 (length) and 0.7 (area) come from the commonly reproduced table; a search summary of a 1974 paper says Teghtsoonian (1965) found 0.76 for circles and 0.80 to 0.83 for irregular shapes. The step from these thresholds to a minimum text-size ratio is this record's inference; a search for studies of font-size discrimination or perceived typographic hierarchy found none.

sources.citation: Gray, P. Psychology (7th ed.), chapter 7.2 Psychophysics (textbook example of a 1/100 Weber fraction for line length).

Solomon, J. A., Morgan, M., & Chubb, C. (2011). Efficiencies for the statistics of size discrimination. Journal of Vision, 11(12):13. (Title recalled from memory; the search summary gave the authors, year and the Weber fractions.)

Smeets, J. B. J., & Brenner, E. (2008). Grasping Weber's law. Current Biology, 18(23), R1089-R1090. (Authors and title recalled from memory; the search summary gave the 0.06 Weber fraction for visual size.)
A 2012 PLOS ONE article that cites a 'commonly agreed' Weber fraction of about 3% for visual length (title and authors not confirmed).
Wikipedia. Stevens's power law (table of exponents: visual length 1.0, visual area 0.7).
Teghtsoonian, M. (1965). The judgment of size. American Journal of Psychology, 78, 392-402.
Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153-181.

entries.caveats: Stevens' exponents come from people giving number estimates; they vary between people and with instructions. A search summary notes that when people judge area they often estimate a length and square it, which changes the exponent. Legibility is a separate question: a size can be clearly different and still too small to read (see type-size-and-x-height).

entries.principle: The golden ratio in controlled studies: a weak average preference at best, and large differences between people
entries.claim: Fechner's 1876 experiment found that the rectangle closest to the golden ratio (1 to 1.618) was chosen most often, by roughly a third of participants. Later work did not confirm a reliable preference. Replications are mixed, a careful repetition found no preference, and studies of individuals find that each person has a stable favourite proportion that differs from person to person. No study found tests the golden ratio on web layouts.
entries.mechanism: The golden ratio is the proportion in which the whole relates to the larger part as the larger part relates to the smaller: (a + b) / a = a / b = 1.618. The belief in its beauty predates the experiments. Three things keep the belief alive. First, Fechner's result is real but depends on his set of ten rectangles: a 1974 study argued that the preferred rectangle depends on its position in the range shown. Second, averaging hides people: one person likes squares, another likes long rectangles, and the average lands in between, near 1.5 to 1.6, without anyone having a special response to 1.618. Third, any admired object contains many possible measurements, so a match can be found after the fact.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — no proportion in the normal range changes effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — group preference is weak and unreliable; individual preferences are strong but differ

designMoves: Choose the aspect ratio of images, cards and columns from the content (the photographs you have, the line length the text needs) and from the device, not from 1.618.
Use a small fixed set of aspect ratios across the site so that repeated elements match.
Treat 1.618 as one acceptable ratio among many between a square and a 2 to 5 rectangle.
antiPatterns: A sidebar-to-content split set to 38% and 62% and defended as 'proven'.
Cropping photographs to 1.618 at the cost of their subject.
A tool that scores a layout higher for containing the golden ratio.

howToCheck.machine: No measurable check of quality exists for the golden ratio, and a program must not award points for it. The measurable property is consistency: compute width / height for every image, card and media block of the same role, round to two decimals, and count the distinct values. Flag roles with more distinct ratios than the Catalog allows. The research gives no preferred ratio and no cap.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether each image and card shows its content without awkward cropping or empty space.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the popular claim that 1.618 is specially pleasing. The studies against it are peer-reviewed but were seen only as search summaries. McManus (1980): the search summary quoted the abstract, which concludes that all the effects in the earlier literature were dubious and reports stable but idiosyncratic individual preferences with two factors, one centred on the square and one on a proportion near the golden section. McManus, Cook and Hunt (2010): 79 participants; weak group preference, strong and stable individual preferences that personality measures did not explain. Höge (1997) repeated Fechner's method and found no preference (reported by secondary sources). A 2010 paper calls the replication record 'a terribly mixed bag'. Fechner's own figure is given as 35% by one secondary source and 34.5% by another: figure not confirmed. Green's (1995) review was not opened; from memory it concludes that real effects may exist but are fragile, which is a milder verdict than 'myth'. The existing record folklore-golden-ratio cites Stieger and Swami (2015) for art pictures.

sources.citation: Fechner, G. T. (1876). Vorschule der Aesthetik. Breitkopf & Härtel.
McManus, I. C. (1980). The aesthetics of simple figures. British Journal of Psychology, 71, 505-524.

McManus, I. C., Cook, R., & Hunt, A. (2010). Beyond the golden section and normative aesthetics: Why do individuals differ so much in their aesthetic preferences for rectangles? Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts, 4(2), 113-126. (Seen through a 2016 article that summarises it.)
Green, C. D. (1995). All that glitters: A review of psychological research on the aesthetics of the golden section. Perception, 24, 937-968.
Höge, H. (1997). The golden section hypothesis: Its last funeral. Empirical Studies of the Arts, 15(2), 233-255.
Phillips, F., Norman, J. F., & Beers, A. M. (2010). Fechner's aesthetics revisited. Seeing and Perceiving, 23(3), 263-271. (Journal details recalled from memory.)

Godkewitsch, M. (1974). The 'golden section': An artifact of stimulus range and measure of preference. American Journal of Psychology, 87, 269-277. (Seen only as a mention in a search summary; journal details recalled from memory.)

entries.caveats: The studies used plain rectangles and art, not pages with content. They show that the special status of 1.618 lacks support; they do not show that proportion is unimportant. The search could not open Green's review, the most thorough one, so its exact conclusion is unconfirmed.

entries.principle: The rule of thirds: tests do not support it; centre and 'facing inward' fit the data better
entries.claim: The rule of thirds says that a picture looks best when its subject sits on one of the lines that divide the frame into thirds. A study of photographs and paintings found no preference for images that follow the rule, and highly rated photographs followed it no more than photographs that ignore it. Experiments on single objects found that people prefer the object at or near the centre, and prefer an object that faces sideways to face into the frame.
entries.mechanism: The rule places the subject at one third or two thirds of the width or height, which is an offset of one third of the half-width from the centre. Palmer and colleagues propose two simpler tendencies. Centre bias: a front-facing object is liked best at the centre, and liking falls evenly on both sides. Inward bias: an object that faces left is liked best when it sits right of centre, so that it faces into the picture, and the reverse for an object that faces right. An off-centre subject that faces inward will often land near a thirds line, which may explain why the rule seems to work.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the studies measured preference only
effects.satisfaction: unknown — no preference for rule-following images was detected

designMoves: For a hero image, place a front-facing subject near the centre of the space the image actually occupies, or place a side-facing subject so that it looks toward the text or the centre.
Choose the crop so that the subject stays visible at every breakpoint; set the focal point explicitly (CSS object-position).
Use the thirds grid as a prompt to try an off-centre crop, not as a test of quality.
antiPatterns: A subject that looks or moves out of the frame, away from the headline.
Rejecting a centred composition because it 'breaks the rule of thirds'.
An automated crop that puts the subject on a thirds line and cuts off part of it.

howToCheck.machine: No measurable check of quality exists for the rule of thirds. A program can compute the subject's horizontal offset o = (x_subject - W / 2) / (W / 2), which runs from -1 to 1 with the thirds lines at about ±0.33, but only when a person or an image model marks the subject, and the offset does not predict ratings. The checks that a program can run are: the marked focal point stays inside the visible crop at every breakpoint, and no text overlaps it.
howToCheck.human: Look at each hero image and ask: is the subject whole, and does it face toward the content?

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the rule as a predictor of quality. Amirshahi, Hayn-Leichsenring, Denzler and Redies (2014, Art & Perception): the search summary reported no detected preference for rule-following images, ratings from 30 participants, and low computed rule-of-thirds values for highly rated photographs and for a large set of paintings. Palmer, Gardner and Wickens (2008, Spatial Vision): centre bias and inward bias for single objects, reported through secondary sources. The Palmer laboratory's own page states that results contradicted the rule's main claims; a 2014 conference abstract from the same group calls the rule 'empirically incorrect' but possibly useful as a nudge away from dead centre. All sources were seen as search summaries. No study on web hero images was found.

sources.citation: Amirshahi, S. A., Hayn-Leichsenring, G. U., Denzler, J., & Redies, C. (2014). Evaluating the rule of thirds in photographs and paintings. Art & Perception, 2(1-2), 163-182.

Palmer, S. E., Gardner, J. S., & Wickens, T. D. (2008). Aesthetic issues in spatial composition: Effects of position and direction on framing single objects. Spatial Vision, 21, 421-449. (Seen through a search summary of J. S. Gardner's 2011 dissertation, which draws on it.)
Palmer Lab, University of California, Berkeley. How the 'Rule of Thirds' is wrong (laboratory web page).

entries.caveats: The experiments used single objects on plain backgrounds and collections of photographs; a web page adds text that competes for the same space. One crowdsourcing report found that people often follow the rule when they crop, which shows a habit, not a benefit. The centre preference concerns one object; scenes with several subjects were not covered.

entries.principle: 4-point and 8-point spacing grids are convention; the measurable benefit is a small, consistent set of values
entries.claim: A spacing grid restricts every margin, padding and gap to multiples of one base unit, usually 4 or 8 pixels. No study found tests 8 against any other number. The grid's value is that it forces a small set of spacing values and keeps related gaps equal, which supports grouping by proximity.
entries.mechanism: With base unit u, every spacing value is k × u for a whole number k. Google's Material Design states that components align to an 8 dp grid and that small elements may use 4 dp. Practitioner articles give an arithmetic reason: multiples of 8 stay whole numbers of device pixels at the common screen scale factors 0.75, 1.5, 2 and 3 (8 × 0.75 = 6, 8 × 1.5 = 12), so edges stay sharp. That reason was found only in informal articles, not in Google's documentation. The perceptual argument is indirect: people group elements by nearness (see proximity-and-common-region), and a short list of clearly different gap sizes makes 'near' and 'far' easy to tell apart. Any base unit gives this benefit.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — no study isolates a spacing grid; consistent gaps plausibly make groups easier to see
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Define a short spacing scale in tokens (for example 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64) and use nothing else.
Make neighbouring steps of the scale clearly different: apply the same ratio thinking as for type sizes (see type-size-step-jnd).
Keep the space inside a group smaller than the space between groups.
Allow documented exceptions for optical corrections (for example aligning an icon with text) instead of bending the scale.
antiPatterns: Spacing values of 13, 15, 17 and 22 pixels scattered through a stylesheet.
Claiming that 8 is 'scientifically' the right unit.
A gap inside a card that is larger than the gap between cards.

howToCheck.machine: Collect every computed margin, padding and gap value above zero. (1) On-grid share = count of values where value mod u = 0, divided by the count of all values, with u from the Prescription (4 by default). Flag a share below the Catalog limit (0.95 is a reasonable start; the research gives no number). (2) Report the count of distinct spacing values and flag a count above the Catalog cap. (3) For each visual group, compute the largest gap inside the group divided by the smallest gap between that group and its neighbours; flag a result of 1 or more.
howToCheck.human: Squint at the page: do the groups separate cleanly, and do equal relationships have equal gaps?

evidence.strengthNote: Vendor guidance and practitioner articles, all seen as search summaries. Material Design's 8 dp grid with 4 dp increments is documented by Google. The device-pixel argument appears only in informal articles. One aggregator traces the 8-point system to Apple and Google guidelines; sources disagree about whether 4 or 8 is the core unit. No experiment comparing base units, and none comparing a grid with free spacing, was found. The grouping argument borrows the evidence of proximity-and-common-region (grade A-), which supports consistent, clearly different gaps but says nothing about the number 8.

sources.citation: Google. Material Design 2: Understanding layout, and Spacing methods (8 dp grid, 4 dp increments).
Spec.fm. 8-Point Grid (practitioner article).
Cieden. How can I choose the right spacing system? (practitioner article).

entries.caveats: CSS pixels are not device pixels, and browsers round fractional values, so the sharp-edge argument is weaker on the web than in native apps. Text does not sit on the grid by itself: line boxes add space above and below letters (see baseline-grid-convention). A grid can make spacing tidy and still wrong if the group structure is wrong.

entries.principle: Baseline grids and 'vertical rhythm' are print craft; no reading study supports them on screens
entries.claim: A baseline grid places every line of text on evenly spaced horizontal lines, so that lines in neighbouring columns align. Articles assert that this improves readability; the search found no controlled study that measures any effect, on paper or on screen. Treat it as an optional craft detail for multi-column text.
entries.mechanism: The grid sets one unit, usually the body line height (for example 24 px for 16 px text at a ratio of 1.5). Every line height and every vertical space is a whole multiple of that unit, so the baselines (the lines on which letters sit) of all text fall on the grid. In print the grid stops text on the two sides of a thin sheet from showing through between lines and keeps columns level. Neither reason applies to a single-column web page. In CSS the baseline's position inside a line box depends on the font's internal metrics, so text of two typefaces or two sizes does not land on a shared grid without per-font corrections.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — no study found
effects.satisfaction: unknown — no study found
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: none — a baseline grid does not change how a reader understands the page

designMoves: Set line heights and vertical spacing as multiples of the spacing base unit; this gives most of the tidiness at no cost.
Align baselines explicitly only where text sits side by side: a label next to a field value, a price next to a product name, columns of body text.
Do not spend effort forcing headings onto the body grid.
antiPatterns: Awkward heading line heights chosen only to stay on the grid.
Promising better readability from vertical rhythm.
Text in adjacent columns that starts at visibly different heights.

howToCheck.machine: Two checks exist, and neither is tied to a measured benefit. (1) Unit check: every computed line-height in pixels mod u = 0, and every vertical margin and padding mod u = 0, where u is the base unit. (2) Side-by-side check: for text elements in the same row (same flex or grid row), compare the first-baseline y positions and flag differences from 1 to 3 pixels, which read as mistakes. Report the result; do not fail a build on check 1.
howToCheck.human: Look across each row of side-by-side text for lines that almost align.

evidence.strengthNote: One search aimed at reading studies of baseline grids returned only tutorials and practitioner articles; they assert a readability benefit without data, and several admit that a grid-aligned layout can still feel wrong. The absence is what this search surfaced, not proof that no study exists. The print origin and the CSS font-metric problem were reported by the same articles. Evidence on line spacing itself (which does matter) is in the existing record spacing-and-justification.

sources.citation: Liew, Z. Why is vertical rhythm an important typography practice? (practitioner article).
SitePoint. Typography: Baseline rhythm deciphered (practitioner article).
Webiano. Baseline grid (knowledge-base article that notes the font-dependent baseline offset).

entries.caveats: Near-miss misalignment of side-by-side text is a visible flaw whether or not a grid exists (see alignment-points-and-near-misses). Newer CSS features for trimming the space above and below text may make strict grids easier; browser support was not checked here.

entries.principle: Alignment is countable: fewer shared edges and no near misses
entries.claim: The number of distinct edge positions on a screen is a measurable property. Screens whose elements share few edge positions (good alignment) and form clear groups were searched faster and preferred in an experiment, and a computed layout score predicted search time. Published interface-aesthetics formulas use the count of alignment points as a term.
entries.mechanism: An alignment point is a distinct x position where at least one element starts (a vertical alignment point) or a distinct y position (a horizontal one). If 20 elements start at 4 x positions, the eye can follow 4 lines; if they start at 17 positions, there are no lines to follow. Aligned edges form lines by good continuation (see alignment-continuity), which lets a person scan down a column. A near miss, where two edges differ by 1 to 3 pixels, is worse than a clear offset: it reads as an error. One published formula, Ngo's 'simplicity', is 3 / (vertical alignment points + horizontal alignment points + number of objects), so fewer points give a higher score.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — search times were shorter on well aligned, well grouped screens
effects.satisfaction: raises — alignment and grouping raised stated preference in the same experiment

designMoves: Give every section the same left edge for text, and reuse a small set of column edges across the page.
Remove near misses: two edges that differ by 1 to 3 pixels must either match or differ clearly.
Align labels, fields and buttons in a form to one or two vertical lines.
When something must be offset, make the offset a full step of the spacing scale.
antiPatterns: Cards whose text starts 2 pixels to the right of the heading above them.
A different left margin in each section.
Centred, left-aligned and right-aligned blocks mixed on one screen without a reason.

howToCheck.machine: Take the bounding boxes of visible text blocks, images and controls in one viewport. (1) Count distinct left-edge x values, distinct right-edge x values and distinct top-edge y values, after merging values within 0.5 pixel. Report alignment ratio = distinct left edges / number of elements; lower is more aligned. The Catalog sets the limit; the research gives no cutoff. (2) Near-miss check: flag every pair of elements in the same container whose left edges (or top edges within a row) differ by 1 to 3 pixels. Check 2 is a firm defect check; check 1 is a comparison between Options.
howToCheck.human: Hold a ruler or a window edge against the screen and look for edges that almost line up.

evidence.strengthNote: Parush, Nadir and Shtub (1998, International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction): a numerical model built from element size, local density, alignment and grouping; well designed screens gave shorter search times and higher preference; model predictions correlated with search times; poor alignment combined with poor local density hurt search time most, and alignment and grouping mainly influenced preference. Seen as a search summary of the abstract and of a secondary summary, which disagree in detail; effect sizes not retrieved. Miniukovich and De Angeli (2015) include layout metrics among eight automatic metrics; the search summary did not list them, and 'grid quality' as one of them is recalled from memory. The Ngo simplicity formula is recalled from memory, not checked. The near-miss rule is a craft rule with no study of its own.

sources.citation: Parush, A., Nadir, R., & Shtub, A. (1998). Evaluating the layout of graphical user interface screens: Validation of a numerical computerized model. International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, 10(4), 343-360.
Ngo, D. C. L., Teo, L. S., & Byrne, J. G. (2003). Modelling interface aesthetics. Information Sciences, 152, 25-46.
Miniukovich, A., & De Angeli, A. (2015). Computation of interface aesthetics. Proceedings of CHI 2015, 1163-1172.

entries.caveats: The 1998 experiment used desktop application screens of its time, not web pages. A low alignment-point count can also describe a monotonous page. Centred layouts create few shared left edges by design; compare like with like. The existing record alignment-continuity covers the perceptual principle; this record adds the counts.

entries.principle: Balance and symmetry can be computed; they predict ratings of simple images better than ratings of real pages
entries.claim: Formulas for balance (equal visual weight on both sides of an axis) and symmetry (one half mirrors the other) exist and are easy to compute from element boxes or pixels. In experiments, people preferred symmetric abstract images, and left-right symmetry raised beauty ratings of website start pages. The formulas track what people call 'balanced' in simple pictures; their link to how much people like a real page is weaker and depends on other properties.
entries.mechanism: Balance treats each element as a weight on a seesaw. Ngo's balance formula gives each side of the screen a weight w = sum of (element area × distance from the element's centre to the screen's centre line). Horizontal balance is then 1 - |w_left - w_right| / max(w_left, w_right): 1 means perfectly balanced, 0 means all weight on one side. The same is done for top against bottom, and the two results are averaged. A pixel version measures how far the centre of 'visual mass' (the darkness-weighted average position of all pixels) lies from the centre of the frame. Mirror symmetry compares the left half with the flipped right half. Symmetric patterns are quick to process, which people tend to experience as pleasant (see processing-fluency-liking).

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — the cited studies measured ratings, not effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — symmetric images and pages received higher beauty ratings on average; the effect on real pages differs between groups of people

designMoves: Balance each viewport: a heavy image on one side needs text, a form or another image of similar weight on the other, or a centred arrangement.
Use left-right symmetry for simple, formal pages (a landing hero, a sign-in page); use balanced asymmetry (text one side, image the other) where content differs.
Reduce the number of separate groups before tuning balance: in one experiment more groups lowered appeal.
antiPatterns: All content pushed to one side with an empty other side at desktop width, with no intent behind it.
Treating a balance score as a quality score.
Forcing symmetry on content that is not symmetric, such as a long text beside a short one.

howToCheck.machine: From the element boxes in one viewport (or from a blurred greyscale screenshot, using darkness as weight): (1) horizontal balance B = 1 - |w_left - w_right| / max(w_left, w_right), with w = sum of area × distance to the vertical centre line; range 0 to 1. (2) Centre-of-mass offset = distance between the weighted centroid and the viewport centre, divided by half the viewport diagonal; range 0 to 1, 0 is centred. (3) Mirror symmetry S = 1 - mean(|I(x, y) - I(W - x, y)|) / 255 on the blurred screenshot; range 0 to 1. Report all three and compare Options within one Template. No validated pass mark exists; flag only extreme values (for example B below 0.5) for a person to look at.
howToCheck.human: Squint or blur the screenshot and ask whether one side feels heavier, and whether that is intended.

entries.caveats: Samples are small (16 to 60 people) and most stimuli were abstract or static. Area is a crude stand-in for visual weight: a small saturated button can outweigh a large pale panel. A page that scrolls has no single frame; compute per viewport. Responsive layouts change balance at each width.

entries.principle: Formulas computed from a screenshot explain at most about half of how people rate a page
entries.claim: Several research teams built automatic metrics of web-page appearance (complexity, colour, symmetry, layout) and tested them against human ratings. The best models explain roughly half of the variation in ratings for web pages and about a third for phone apps. A computed score is useful for comparing versions and for flagging outliers. It cannot certify that a page looks good.
entries.mechanism: Each team turns a screenshot into numbers: amount of detail, number and spread of colours, count of text and image areas, symmetry, alignment. A regression then weights the numbers to fit average human ratings. The share of variation that the fitted model reproduces is called variance explained (R squared); 0.5 means that half of the differences between pages' ratings follow the model and half do not. The unexplained half includes content, imagery, brand, the viewer's own taste and culture, and whatever the metrics fail to capture. Because the weights are fitted to one set of pages from one period, they fit new pages and newer styles less well.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — the models predict appeal ratings, not effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the models predict first-impression ratings of screenshots, not satisfaction after use

designMoves: Use computed metrics to compare Options within one Template and to catch extremes, and say so in the Honest receipt.
Report each metric separately (complexity, colour count, symmetry) instead of one blended 'beauty score'.
Keep a person's judgment as the final step for visual appeal.
antiPatterns: A single aesthetic score presented as a verdict.
Optimising a page toward a metric until it looks empty.
Applying weights fitted to websites from 2013 to a modern design as if they were constants of nature.

howToCheck.machine: Compute each metric on the same viewport sizes for every Option and for the Template baseline, then report the difference from the baseline in standard deviations: z = (value - baseline mean) / baseline standard deviation. Flag |z| above 2 for a person to review. Do not convert the metrics into a pass or fail for appeal: with R squared near 0.5, the prediction error for a single page stays large (the unexplained share of variation is 1 - R squared, about half).
howToCheck.human: Collect a quick rating from the owner or a few people on the Catalog's appeal question; that rating, not the formula, decides.

Ratings were averaged over people, so the models predict the average viewer better than any one viewer, and this tool serves one owner. entries.principle: Birkhoff's formula (beauty = order ÷ complexity) is famous and failed its tests
entries.claim: In 1933 the mathematician George Birkhoff proposed that aesthetic measure M equals order O divided by complexity C. Experiments from the 1930s onward found little or no agreement between M and what people actually prefer. The formula should not drive any check. The useful remainder is the idea that both order and complexity matter.
entries.mechanism: Birkhoff reasoned that complexity costs the viewer effort and order rewards it, so pleasure is the reward per unit of effort: M = O / C. For polygons he defined C as the number of distinct straight lines that contain the sides, and O as a sum of points for vertical symmetry, balance, rotational symmetry and fit to a horizontal-vertical grid, minus points for awkward features. The formula makes the simplest ordered figure the best; the square scores highest among polygons. People do not judge that way: very simple figures bore them. Eysenck tested the formula, found low correlations with ratings, and proposed the opposite relation, M = O × C, in which complexity adds to appeal when order is present.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — the formula was tested against preference only
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the formula's predictions correlated poorly with ratings

designMoves: Treat order (alignment, repetition, symmetry, consistency) and complexity (amount and variety of elements) as two separate dials, and report them separately.
Raise order first; then decide how much complexity the content and the genre need.
Do not divide one by the other.
antiPatterns: An 'aesthetic score' computed as order divided by complexity.
Citing Birkhoff as proof that the simplest design is the most beautiful.
Removing content to raise a ratio.

howToCheck.machine: No measurable check should use M = O / C or M = O × C; neither predicts ratings reliably. Compute order measures (see alignment-points-and-near-misses, balance-and-symmetry-metrics) and complexity measures (see complexity-measures-and-preference-curve) and report them side by side.
howToCheck.human: Ask two separate questions: is the page orderly, and is there enough on it to be interesting and useful?

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the formula as a predictor of preference. Birkhoff's formula is a theoretical proposal. A 2023 paper by Hübner and Ufken states that later empirical studies found little support for M and cites Davis (1936), Beebe-Center and Pratt (1937), Wilson (1939) and McWhinnie (1968); a 2010 paper by Nadal and colleagues reports that Eysenck (1941) found considerably low correlations between predicted M and beauty ratings; another secondary source reports Eysenck's alternative M = O × C. All of this was seen as search summaries of secondary sources; none of the original papers was opened, and no correlation values were retrieved. The polygon definitions of O and C and the square's top score are recalled from memory.

entries.principle: Visual complexity can be measured by compressed file size; on websites, liking mostly falls as complexity rises
entries.claim: The size of a compressed screenshot is a cheap, valid measure of how complex people judge a page to be: in one study, JPEG file size correlated 0.80 with complexity ratings. Classic theory predicts that people like a medium level of complexity best (an inverted U). Studies of websites mostly find a simpler pattern: the less complex page is liked more. One study with three levels found the inverted U.
entries.mechanism: Compression removes repetition. A screenshot with large flat areas and repeated shapes compresses to few bytes; one with many different edges, textures and colours does not. So bytes per pixel after compression estimates the amount of non-repeating visual detail. Other measures count edges directly (edge density: the share of pixels that an edge detector marks) or measure how much local variation in colour, contrast and orientation a new item would have to compete with (feature congestion; see clutter-and-crowding). Berlyne's theory says liking rises with complexity up to an optimum and then falls. A common explanation for the mostly downward results on websites is that real web pages already sit past the optimum, on the falling side of the curve. A second explanation is that people differ: some like simple and some like complex, and the average hides both.

effects.cognitiveLoad: raises — more complex pages are harder to search (see clutter-and-crowding)
effects.satisfaction: lowers — higher complexity went with lower appeal ratings in most website studies; one study found a medium level best
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not measured in the cited sources

designMoves: Measure complexity for every Option and prefer the lower value when the content is the same.
Lower complexity by removing variety (fewer colours, fewer type styles, fewer box treatments) before removing content.
Watch the low end as well: a near-empty first viewport can look unfinished or cheap (see simplicity-can-read-as-cheap).
antiPatterns: Photographic backgrounds, gradients and textures stacked under text.
Treating 'less is always better' as a law; the evidence is an average trend with exceptions.
Comparing file sizes of screenshots taken at different sizes, formats or quality settings.

howToCheck.machine: Render the first viewport at a fixed size (for example 1280 by 800 and 390 by 844), save it as JPEG at one fixed quality setting, and compute complexity = file bytes / (width × height). Optionally add edge density = edge pixels / all pixels from a Canny edge detector with fixed thresholds. Compare with the Template baseline: flag values more than 2 standard deviations above it as 'busy' and more than 2 below as 'possibly empty'. No absolute threshold exists in the research; the settings must stay identical between runs, because the number depends on them.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether anything on the page could be removed or made the same as its neighbours without losing meaning.

evidence.strengthNote: Seen as search summaries, one of which quoted the abstract. Donderi (2006) proposed compressed file size as a complexity measure; its coefficient was not retrieved. These three were reported by secondary sources. The 'falling side of the curve' explanation is the secondary sources' reading, not a tested result.

entries.principle: Perceptual colour spaces (CIELAB, OKLab): equal numeric steps look roughly equal; HSL steps do not
entries.claim: CIELAB and OKLab are colour spaces built so that the straight-line distance between two colours approximates how different they look. In these spaces an even ramp of lightness values looks even, and two colours with the same lightness number look equally light. HSL and HSV lack this property: pure yellow and pure blue both have HSL lightness 50%, but their OKLab lightness is 0.97 and 0.45.
entries.mechanism: Screen colours are stored as sRGB numbers, which describe the signal sent to the display, not the sensation. A perceptual space converts them in four steps: undo the display curve to get linear light; convert to estimates of the three cone responses of the eye; apply a compressive curve (a cube root) because sensation grows more slowly than light; then recombine into one lightness axis L and two colour axes a (green to red) and b (blue to yellow). OKLab does exactly this: a matrix to cone space, a cube root, a second matrix. OKLCH is the same space written as lightness L, chroma C = square root of (a² + b²), and hue h = the angle of (a, b). The colour difference is the distance: delta E = square root of (delta L² + delta a² + delta b²). CIELAB (1976) uses the same idea with a cube-root formula on CIE XYZ values, and is known to bend hues, most visibly blue toward purple, when chroma or lightness changes. OKLab (2020) was fitted to reduce that.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — no user study of ramps built in a perceptual space was found
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured

designMoves: Build every colour ramp in OKLCH: fix the hue, step the lightness L evenly, and adjust chroma to stay inside the screen's gamut (the range of colours it can show).
Give the same step number the same L across hues, so that 'blue 500' and 'green 500' carry equal visual weight.
Make tokens that should look different differ by a clear delta E, and merge tokens that differ by less than the eye can see.
After building a ramp perceptually, still verify text pairs with the WCAG contrast formula (see wcag-contrast-formula-anatomy).
antiPatterns: Ramps made by changing HSL lightness in equal steps.
Two grey tokens one hex digit apart.
Assuming equal OKLCH lightness guarantees equal WCAG contrast; the two use different formulas.

howToCheck.machine: Convert every colour token from sRGB to OKLab (linearise each channel; convert to cone space with the published matrix; take cube roots; apply the second published matrix). For each ramp: (1) L must rise or fall monotonically; (2) evenness = largest L step / smallest L step, flag above 1.5 (the Catalog owns this limit; the research gives none); (3) hue drift = largest h - smallest h in degrees, report it. For all tokens: (4) delta E OK = square root of (delta L² + delta a² + delta b²) between every pair; flag pairs below 0.02 as indistinguishable duplicates. Example: #f5f5f5 against #f4f4f4 gives 0.003. (5) Across hues at the same step number, flag an L spread above 0.05.
howToCheck.human: View each ramp as a row of swatches and look for a step that jumps or two steps that look the same.

evidence.strengthNote: The OKLab construction, matrices and comparison table were read in the author's own post (its source file on GitHub; the last 3% of the file was not read). In the author's test, OKLab's lightness error (root mean square 0.20) and chroma error (0.81) were lower than CIELAB's (1.70 and 1.84) and far lower than HSV's (11.59 and 3.38); hue error was 0.49 against CIELAB's 0.69. Two limits apply: the author ran the comparison himself, and the lightness and chroma test data were generated by another colour model (CAM16), not collected from people, as the post states. A 2026 preprint, seen as a search summary, argues that a different space is more uniform than OKLab. The CSS Color 4 specification, read in part, defines delta E OK as the plain distance in OKLab. The 0.02 just-noticeable value for delta E OK is recalled from that specification's gamut-mapping text and was not found in the part read: figure not confirmed. For CIELAB, a just-noticeable difference of about 1 by design, and about 2.3 in a 1994 study by Mahy and colleagues, come from a search summary of encyclopaedia mirrors: figures not confirmed. CIELAB's hue shift in blues is reported by secondary sources seen in a search summary. The yellow and blue example values were computed here from the published matrices and the standard sRGB conversion matrix, which is recalled from memory.

A colour's look also changes with its neighbours (see simultaneous-contrast). Equal lightness steps do not give equal contrast-ratio steps. The existing record lightness-does-the-work says to build ramps in OKLCH; this record adds the conversion, the distance formula and the numeric checks.

entries.principle: The WCAG 2 contrast ratio: the exact formula, where its constants come from, and where it misleads
entries.claim: The WCAG 2 contrast ratio is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 and L2 are the relative luminance of the lighter and the darker colour. It runs from 1 to 21. It is the legal and standard measure and the project's floor. It is also a simple model: it gives the same result when text and background swap, it ignores text size and weight except for one large-text rule, and critics report that it overstates the contrast of very dark pairs. No peer-reviewed comparison of the formula with people's reading performance was found.
entries.mechanism: Relative luminance is the brightness of a colour on a scale from 0 (black) to 1 (white). To compute it, divide each 8-bit sRGB channel by 255; if the result c is 0.04045 or less use c / 12.92, otherwise use ((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4; then L = 0.2126 × R + 0.7152 × G + 0.0722 × B. The weights reflect that the eye is most sensitive to green and least to blue. The power curve undoes the encoding of sRGB. The 0.05 added to both colours stands for stray light reflected by the screen ('viewing flare'); it also keeps the ratio finite for black, which is why the maximum is 1.05 / 0.05 = 21. The thresholds: 3 to 1 comes from older display standards for people with normal vision; 4.5 is 3 multiplied by 1.5, the contrast-sensitivity loss the W3C associates with 20/40 vision. Because the formula is a ratio of two luminances, it has no term for which colour is the text, for letter thickness, or for the surrounding page.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — text that passes is easier to resolve for most readers; the formula itself is a proxy, not a measurement of effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not measured
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: none — contrast decides whether text can be read, not whether the interface is understood

designMoves: Keep the WCAG 2 ratio as the floor: 4.5 for body text, 3 for large text and for control boundaries, 7 for long reading where possible.
Add margin where the formula is weakest: thin or small text, dark themes with dark-grey text on near-black, and mid-tone coloured buttons. Check those pairs by eye on a real phone.
For a mid-tone background, test both white and black text and look at both; the formula and the eye can disagree there.
Record the measured ratio in the Honest receipt as 'measured', and readability of the weak cases as 'still needs a person'.
antiPatterns: Treating 4.51 as readable and 4.49 as unreadable.
Thin 12 px text that passes 4.5 and is declared fine.
Dark-grey text on black that meets a ratio and is hard to read in daylight.
Skipping the standard formula because a newer model disagrees with it.

howToCheck.machine: For each text and background pair: linearise the channels (c / 12.92 if c ≤ 0.04045, else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4), compute L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, then ratio = (L_lighter + 0.05) / (L_darker + 0.05). Range 1 to 21. Fail below 4.5 for body text, below 3 for large text (24 px, or about 18.67 px bold) and for control boundaries. Reference values: #767676 on white = 4.54 (pass), #777777 on white = 4.48 (fail), white on #ff8000 = 2.52, black on #ff8000 = 8.34. Additional warning with no validated threshold: list passing pairs in which both colours have L below 0.18, and passing pairs with text under 16 px or font weight under 400, for a person to check.
howToCheck.human: Read the listed weak pairs on a phone outdoors and on a dim screen. Confirm white-on-colour buttons by eye.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade A covers the formula and thresholds as a standard: the WCAG definitions of relative luminance and contrast ratio and the explanation of criterion 1.4.3 were read from the W3C source repository. They state the coefficients, the 0.04045 threshold (0.03928 before May 2021, with no practical effect), the 0.05 flare term 'based on Typical Viewing Flare' from a draft of the sRGB standard, the origin of the ratio in ISO 9241-3 and ANSI/HFES 100-1988, and the 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 derivation. The weaknesses have weaker support (grade C): they come from a W3C issue thread, a university blog, and a 2022 article by Sam Waller of the Cambridge Engineering Design Centre, all seen as search summaries. Waller reports that he found no traceable empirical or theoretical evidence for the formula as a predictor of legibility, and that for mid-grey backgrounds (levels of about 118 to 168) the WCAG formula and the newer APCA model disagree about whether black or white text is better. That is a comparison of two formulas, not a test with readers. A search for a peer-reviewed study that compares either formula with reading speed found none. The symmetry of the ratio and the reference values were computed here.

This project does not use the apca-w3 package (its licence prohibits commercial use), and WCAG 2 remains the standard that laws cite.
