entries.principle: Colour harmony: experiments favour similar hue and a clear lightness difference, not colour-wheel geometry
entries.claim: Colour-wheel schemes (complementary, triadic, analogous) are design tradition. When experiments ask people to rate pairs of colours, harmony rises as the two hues become more similar, and with a moderate difference in lightness; lighter pairs rate higher. Complementary pairs give strong contrast, which people do not rate as harmonious. Harmony and preference are different judgments, and people differ widely.
entries.mechanism: A colour-wheel scheme picks hues by angle: complementary 180 degrees apart, triadic 120 degrees, analogous within about 30 degrees. Moon and Spencer (1944) turned the tradition into mathematics: pairs are harmonious when their difference in hue, lightness or chroma falls in zones called identity, similarity or contrast, and unpleasant when it falls in the 'ambiguous' zones between; they also proposed a balance rule for areas. Later tests questioned those zones. Ou and Luo (2006) instead fitted a model to ratings of 1,431 colour pairs. Its terms are a chromatic-difference term, a lightness-sum term (lighter pairs harmonise more), a lightness-difference term (a moderate difference helps; very small differences hurt) and a hue term. Schloss and Palmer (2011) separated three questions: how much people like a pair, how harmonious they find it, and how much they like a figure on a background. Harmony followed hue similarity most closely.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — harmony ratings are not a measure of effort
effects.satisfaction: raises — similar-hue pairs with a clear lightness difference are rated more harmonious and, on average, liked more; liking depends more on whether the person likes each colour

designMoves: Build the neutral and surface colours from one hue family (or one hue plus greys), and separate them by lightness.
Use a contrasting or complementary hue for one job only: the accent that must stand out. Contrast serves attention, not harmony.
Keep background pairs light; the tested models rate lighter combinations as more harmonious.
Ask the owner whether they like each colour by itself; liking for the parts strongly affects liking for the pair.
antiPatterns: A triadic palette used at equal strength because a colour-wheel tool called it harmonious.
Two adjacent surfaces that differ slightly in lightness and also in hue, which looks like an error.
Citing a harmony formula as proof that a palette is good.

howToCheck.machine: Convert the palette's main surfaces and brand colours to OKLCH (or CIELAB). For each pair that touches in the layout, report hue difference dh = the smaller angle between the two hues (0 to 180 degrees; ignore it when either chroma is near zero) and the lightness difference dL. Label pairs with dh up to 30 as 'similar hue', 150 to 180 as 'complementary'. Flag adjacent surface pairs with dh above 30 and a CIELAB lightness difference under about 15 as likely to clash; the 15 figure comes from a secondary summary and is not confirmed. No validated pass or fail exists for harmony; report, do not gate.
howToCheck.human: Ask the owner to rate each main colour pair for 'goes together' and, separately, for 'I like it'.

evidence.strengthNote: All seen as search summaries. Ou and Luo (2006, Color Research and Application): 1,431 pairs rated on a 10-category scale; the model was tested on an independent data set with 'satisfactory' performance; the term names and the equal-hue, high-lightness and moderate-lightness-difference principles were reported by citing papers; the model's equations were not retrieved. Schloss and Palmer (2011): 32 colours, 992 pairs; preference and harmony both rose with hue similarity; average ratings of preference and harmony correlated +.79, while the correlation within single participants ranged from -.03 to +.70 (figures from a secondary account). The statement about complementary pairs follows from the hue-similarity result and was not seen stated directly. Moon and Spencer (1944): a study of 390 combinations with 31 participants found their zones 'questionable'; an earlier study found that people followed Munsell's area rule more than theirs. No study of colour-wheel schemes on web pages was found.

sources.citation: Ou, L.-C., & Luo, M. R. (2006). A colour harmony model for two-colour combinations. Color Research and Application, 31(3), 191-204. (Volume and pages recalled from memory.)

Schloss, K. B., & Palmer, S. E. (2011). Aesthetic response to color combinations: Preference, harmony, and similarity. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 73(2), 551-571. (Volume and pages recalled from memory.)
Moon, P., & Spencer, D. E. (1944). Aesthetic measure applied to color harmony. Journal of the Optical Society of America, 34(4), 234-242.

Chuang, M.-C., & Ou, L.-C. (2001). Influence of a holistic color interval on color harmony. Color Research and Application, 26(1), 29-39. (Authors and title recalled from memory; the search summary gave the 390 combinations, the 31 participants and the conclusion.)

entries.caveats: The experiments rated two flat patches side by side, not a page with text, images and proportions. Ratings are averages; individual taste and culture vary (see preferences-vary-by-audience). The models describe 'harmony', which is not the same as 'appropriate for this business' (see color-fit-and-brand-personality).

entries.principle: Folklore: 'the 60-30-10 rule makes a palette balanced'
entries.claim: The 60-30-10 rule says to give a dominant colour 60% of the area, a secondary colour 30% and an accent 10%. It comes from interior-decorating advice. No study, and no documented origin, was found for the numbers. The structure behind it (one quiet dominant colour, a supporting colour, a sparing accent) agrees with evidence about attention; the percentages are arbitrary.
entries.mechanism: The rule works as a memory aid for hierarchy among colours. Its sound core rests on other findings: an accent attracts the eye only when it is rare (see preattentive-popout), and pages with fewer competing colours are rated better at first sight (see low-complexity-high-prototypicality). Neither finding gives 60, 30 or 10. On a typical web page the neutral background and text already take far more than 60% of the area, and an accent used for calls to action takes far less than 10%.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — the rule itself was never tested; a rare accent does make the main action easier to find
effects.satisfaction: unknown — no study found

designMoves: Assign roles, not percentages: one dominant neutral for surfaces, one supporting colour for structure, one accent for the things that must be found.
Keep the accent rare enough that it stays a signal; measure its share instead of assuming 10%.
State in the Prescription that the split is a convention.
antiPatterns: Adding a coloured band to a page only to bring the secondary colour up to 30%.
An accent colour used on so many elements that none of them stands out.
Telling the owner that the 60-30-10 split is proven.

howToCheck.machine: No measurable check exists for the 60-30-10 numbers. A program can measure the roles: take a screenshot of each main viewport, assign every pixel to the nearest palette token by OKLab distance, and report each role's share of pixels. Flag an accent share above the Catalog limit (the research gives no number; 10% is the convention) and report when no single colour role exceeds 50%.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether the accent still points to the most important action on each screen.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade D applies to the specific percentages. One search aimed at the rule's origin and at any empirical test returned only decorating magazines and marketing articles; they assert that the rule comes from interior design and has been used 'for decades', cite no source, and call it a guide. Its transfer to interfaces is presented in those articles as advice, without tests. The absence of a study is what one search surfaced. The supporting evidence about rare accents and few colours belongs to other records and has higher grades.

sources.citation: Livingetc. A decorator's guide to the 60-30-10 rule and how to use it to create your color scheme (magazine article).
Apartment Therapy. How design pros use the 60-30-10 rule to create balance (magazine article).

entries.caveats: Moon and Spencer (1944) and Munsell proposed formulas that balance colour areas against their strength; tests of those were mixed (see color-harmony-models), and neither produces 60-30-10. Pixel shares depend on the viewport and on photographs, which do not belong to any palette role; exclude image areas or report them separately.

entries.principle: Fitts's law as a formula: what it computes, typical values, and why touch needs a correction
entries.claim: Movement time to a target is MT = a + b × log2(D / W + 1), where D is the distance to the target and W is its width along the direction of movement. The log term is the index of difficulty, in bits. The formula predicts well for a mouse or stylus. For a finger on a touchscreen it under-predicts the difficulty of small targets, because a finger adds a fixed imprecision that does not shrink when the person slows down.
entries.mechanism: The index of difficulty ID = log2(D / W + 1) grows when the target is farther or smaller, and it grows by one bit each time D / W + 1 doubles. The constants a (seconds) and b (seconds per bit) are fitted to data for one device and one person or group; b for a mouse is about 0.1 second per bit in the classic study. Because of the logarithm, gains shrink: at a distance of 400 px, widening a target from 24 to 48 px cuts ID from 4.14 to 3.22 bits (about 0.09 second at b = 0.1), and widening again to 96 px cuts it to 2.37. Researchers compare devices by throughput = ID / MT in bits per second, using an 'effective width' of 4.133 × the standard deviation of where people actually landed. For touch, Bi, Li and Zhai proposed FFitts law: MT = a + b × log2(D / square root of (2 × pi × e × (sigma² - sigma_a²)) + 1), where sigma is the spread of touch points and sigma_a is the finger's fixed imprecision. When the target is small, sigma_a dominates and enlarging the target is the only fix.

effects.cognitiveLoad: none — the law describes movement, not thinking
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not part of the law
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not part of the law

designMoves: Compare two layouts by the summed index of difficulty of a scripted task, not by absolute predicted seconds.
Spend size on small targets first: the first doubling of a small target saves the most.
On touch, set a minimum physical size (see target-size-in-millimetres) before applying Fitts's law at all.
Shorten D for the next likely action by placing it near the current one.
antiPatterns: Quoting predicted milliseconds as facts without fitted constants for the device and audience.
Using Fitts's law to justify a very large primary button while small secondary targets stay tiny.
Applying the mouse form of the law to thumb use on a phone.

howToCheck.machine: For each step of a scripted task, take D = centre-to-centre distance in CSS pixels from the previous target and W = the smaller of the target's width and height (a conservative choice). Compute ID = log2(D / W + 1) and sum it over the task. Report the sum per Option; a lower sum is better. Flag single steps with ID above the Catalog limit (the research gives no universal limit; mouse studies commonly test 1 to 6 bits). Do not report absolute times unless a and b were measured; with b = 0.1 to 0.2 second per bit, one bit is roughly 0.1 to 0.2 second. For touch, do not use the FFitts formula in a check: it needs measured touch data and fails mathematically when sigma_a exceeds sigma.
howToCheck.human: Time one person performing the scripted task on a phone and on a laptop; compare Options, not predictions.

evidence.strengthNote: The law is among the most replicated results in human-computer interaction; the specifics here were seen as search summaries. The 'Shannon' form with + 1 is MacKenzie's and is the form in ISO 9241-9, which also defines throughput as ID / MT with effective width. MacKenzie's 2003 reanalysis reports that the classic mouse study (Card, English and Burr, 1978) fitted MT = 1.03 + 0.096 ID seconds. The 4.133 factor equals the square root of 2 × pi × e (computed here; a search summary also states it). FFitts law (Bi, Li and Zhai, CHI 2013) and its formula come from a search summary. Ko and colleagues (2021) report that the FFitts formula breaks when the value under the square root is negative and that nominal width sometimes predicts better. The 0.1 to 0.2 second-per-bit range and the 1 to 6 bit range are recalled from memory, not checked. The worked numbers were computed here.

sources.citation: MacKenzie, I. S., & Soukoreff, R. W. (2003). Card, English, and Burr (1978): 25 years later. Extended Abstracts of CHI 2003. (Authors and title recalled from memory; the search summary gave the regression equation and the throughput reanalysis.)
Wikipedia. Fitts's law (Shannon formulation, ISO 9241-9 index of difficulty and throughput).
Bi, X., Li, Y., & Zhai, S. (2013). FFitts law: Modeling finger touch with Fitts' law. Proceedings of CHI 2013, 1363-1372.

Ko, Y.-J., Zhao, H., Ramakrishnan, I. V., Zhai, S., & Bi, X. (2021). Issues related to using Finger-Fitts law to model one-dimensional touch pointing tasks. Chinese CHI 2021. (Author list recalled from memory.)
Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 47(6), 381-391.

entries.caveats: The law predicts the movement only; finding the target and deciding take additional time (see hick-hyman-formula). W is the size along the line of approach, and for two-dimensional targets researchers disagree about which dimension to use. The existing record fitts-and-steering covers the design consequences and the steering law; this record adds the arithmetic.

entries.principle: The Hick-Hyman law as a formula: decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of choices, under narrow conditions
entries.claim: For a practised person choosing among n equally likely, well known alternatives, decision time is RT = a + b × log2(n + 1). Each doubling of the choices adds a constant time, commonly quoted as about 150 milliseconds. The formula does not describe reading through an unfamiliar menu, where time grows in a straight line with the number of items. By its own arithmetic, the formula favours one broad menu over several narrow levels.
entries.mechanism: The term log2(n + 1) is the information in the choice, in bits; the + 1 stands for the uncertainty about whether to respond at all. Hyman's general form is RT = a + b × H, with H = the sum over all alternatives of p × log2(1 / p), where p is how likely each alternative is; frequent choices are faster. The constant b is the time per bit. The law holds when the person already knows where each option is and what it means, as with a familiar keyboard or a menu used daily. A newcomer must read items one by one, which is visual search, not choice among known alternatives. Arithmetic for menus: 16 options in one list cost log2(17) = 4.09 bits; the same 16 in two levels of 4 cost 2 × log2(5) = 4.64 bits plus a second fixed cost a and a second pointing movement. For 64 options: one list 6.02 bits, two levels of 8 6.34 bits, three levels of 4 6.97 bits.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — the law predicts time, not felt effort
effects.satisfaction: unknown — not part of the law
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: unknown — not part of the law

designMoves: Do not cut useful options to save decision time; the logarithm makes each extra option cheap, and extra levels cost more than extra items.
Help newcomers search: order lists by a rule people know (alphabet, time, size), group them, and label them clearly.
Keep positions stable so that repeat visitors can decide from memory.
Put the most likely choice first or make it the default; likely choices carry less information and are faster.
antiPatterns: 'Hick's law says fewer choices are better' used to hide navigation behind extra clicks.
Predicting menu times for first-time visitors with the logarithmic formula.
Reordering menu items between visits.

howToCheck.machine: For each decision point on a scripted path, count the visible options n and compute bits = log2(n + 1). Report the path total: total bits and number of decision points. When comparing two navigation structures for the same content, prefer the one with fewer decision points unless its lists are unsorted and ungrouped. No threshold on n comes from this law. Do not convert bits to seconds for first-time visitors; for them, report the item count per list, because search time grows roughly in proportion to it.
howToCheck.human: Watch one first-time visitor and one repeat visitor find the same three items; note where each hesitates.

evidence.strengthNote: The law itself rests on classic experiments (Hick 1952; Hyman 1953), cited from memory. The formula with n + 1, Hyman's entropy form, and the slope of about 150 milliseconds per bit (one source gives 150 to 200, varying with task and practice) come from a search summary of encyclopaedia and glossary pages, not from the original papers: figures not confirmed against a primary source, hence grade B. The limits for menus are documented in the existing record hick-hyman-limits (Liu and colleagues 2020; Cockburn, Gutwin and Greenberg 2007). The reading of the + 1 as uncertainty about whether to respond is recalled from memory. The breadth-against-depth arithmetic was computed here from the formula.

sources.citation: Wikipedia. Hick's law (formula, entropy form, typical slope).
Usability First glossary. Hick's law (T = k × H with k about 150 ms).
Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 4(1), 11-26.
Hyman, R. (1953). Stimulus information as a determinant of reaction time. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 45(3), 188-196.

entries.caveats: With practice and with natural stimulus-response pairings the slope b falls toward zero, so the law overstates the cost for experts as well. Real choices are rarely equally likely. The law says nothing about the quality of a decision or about regret (see choice-overload). The existing record hick-hyman-limits states the limits; this record adds the formula and the menu arithmetic.

entries.principle: Target size is a physical quantity: convert CSS pixels to millimetres before judging a touch target
entries.claim: The one target-size study that the W3C lists found that thumb targets of 9.2 mm (single taps) and 9.6 mm (sequences of taps) were large enough. A CSS pixel is 0.26 mm only at the reference viewing distance of a desktop screen; on a phone it is about 0.16 mm. So 24 CSS pixels (the WCAG minimum) is about 3.8 mm on a phone, 44 pixels is about 7 mm, 48 pixels is about 7.6 mm, and the study's 9.2 mm needs about 58 CSS pixels.
entries.mechanism: CSS defines 1 px as 1/96 inch at a reference distance of 28 inches (71 cm), which is a visual angle of about 0.0213 degrees. Devices held closer use physically smaller CSS pixels so that content keeps the same apparent size: Android defines its unit (dp) as 1/160 inch, or 0.159 mm, and a typical iPhone shows 163 points per inch, or 0.156 mm per point. Touch accuracy depends on physical size, because the fingertip and its contact patch do not shrink with the screen's pixel density. The formula is size in mm = size in CSS px × k, with k = physical viewport width in mm / viewport width in CSS px (about 0.16 for phones, 0.26 for a desktop monitor at arm's length). Platform minimums of 44 points (Apple) and 48 dp (Google) therefore come to about 7 to 7.6 mm, below the 9.2 mm of the laboratory study.

effects.cognitiveLoad: lowers — fewer missed taps mean fewer corrections
effects.satisfaction: unknown — the study combined participants' ratings with tap accuracy to reach its sizes; no separate satisfaction result was retrieved

designMoves: Treat 24 by 24 CSS pixels as the legal floor, 44 to 48 as the working minimum on phones, and about 58 to 60 (roughly 9 to 9.6 mm) as the size for primary actions used with a thumb.
Where the visible control must stay small, enlarge its tappable area with padding.
Keep at least the WCAG spacing between small adjacent targets.
Judge the size at the phone viewport, not at desktop width.
antiPatterns: Assuming a 44 px button is 11.6 mm because 1 px is 1/96 inch; that conversion holds for the desktop reference pixel only.
Icon buttons of 24 px placed edge to edge on a phone.
Quoting finger-width figures (16 to 20 mm) as a requirement; their source is disputed.

howToCheck.machine: At a phone viewport, read the bounding box of every interactive element and take s = the smaller of its width and height in CSS pixels. Convert: mm = s × k, with k = 0.16 by default or the device's own value (physical screen width in mm / viewport width in CSS px). Fail below 24 px unless the WCAG 2.5.8 spacing exception applies. Warn below 44 px (about 7 mm). For controls the Prescription marks as primary, report whether mm reaches 9.2. Report the share of all targets in each band.
howToCheck.human: Use the page one-handed with a thumb on a real phone; note every missed or doubled tap.

evidence.strengthNote: The CSS definitions (1 px = 1/96 inch; 0.0213 degrees at 28 inches; about 0.26 mm at arm's length) were read in the CSS Values and Units specification source. WCAG's explanation of criterion 2.5.8 was read: it says the working group reviewed research that mostly concerns touch and suggests larger sizes, chose 24 px as a floor for all pointer types, and it lists one study, Parhi, Karlson and Bederson (2006). That study's 9.2 mm and 9.6 mm figures come from a search summary that quoted its abstract; the sample size was not retrieved, and it is a single study of one-handed thumb use on a small device. The phone conversion factors rest on unit definitions and device densities recalled from memory (Android dp = 1/160 inch; iPhone 163 points per inch) and on arithmetic done here. Secondary sources say that 48 dp is 'about 9 mm'; the unit definition gives 7.6 mm, so that statement is not confirmed. Finger-size figures attributed to the MIT Touch Lab (fingertip 8 to 10 mm, finger pad 10 to 14 mm, index finger 16 to 20 mm) appear only in secondary articles that disagree, and one commenter disputes that the cited paper contains them.

sources.citation: W3C CSS Working Group. CSS Values and Units Module Level 3, editor's draft source (absolute lengths and the reference pixel; section read).
W3C. Understanding Success Criterion 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum).
Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K., & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. Proceedings of MobileHCI 2006, 203-210.
W3C Mobile Accessibility Task Force wiki. Proposed SC Target Size (notes that Apple's point is a density-independent unit, not a physical one).
Nielsen Norman Group. Touch targets on touchscreens (cites a 1 cm by 1 cm minimum and an MIT Touch Lab finger-size figure).

entries.caveats: The factor k differs between devices and changes when the user zooms or sets a larger display size; 0.16 is a typical value, not a constant. The 2006 study used a small handheld device of its time, and its participants' ages were not retrieved; people with tremor or reduced dexterity need more than its figures. An unpublished replication, seen as a secondary source, reported a smaller minimum (6.8 mm). The existing record touch-target-size covers the WCAG criteria; this record adds the physical conversion.

entries.principle: Line height, line length and font size: ratios are convention, and no formula that links them has support
entries.claim: Typographers hold that longer lines need more space between lines, and several published formulas compute an 'ideal' line height from font size and line width, one of them from the golden ratio. The search found no experiment that supports any such formula. What evidence exists is older print research that found one combination best for one type size, plus the accessibility standard's value of 1.5 times the font size.
entries.mechanism: Line height is expressed as a ratio: line height / font size (for example 24 px / 16 px = 1.5). The craft argument for linking it to line length is the return sweep: at the end of a line the eye jumps back to the start of the next one, and on a long line a tight gap makes it easy to land on the wrong line. Tinker and Paterson's print studies, as secondary sources report them, found that for 10-point type a line of about 19 picas (80 mm) with 2 points of extra space (a ratio of 1.2) read best, with a wide 'safety zone' of 14 to 31 picas; other researchers of the period disagreed. The golden-ratio formulas multiply the font size by 1.618 and then adjust for width; they give a derivation, not a test. One practitioner analysis argues that the right basis is the x-height (the height of lowercase letters) and the number of characters per line, not the font size.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — no study tests a formula; very tight spacing on long lines plausibly causes line-skipping
effects.satisfaction: unknown — see spacing-and-justification for preference results on line spacing itself
effects.perceivedIntuitiveness: none — these ratios do not change how the page is understood

designMoves: Set body text at a line-height ratio of about 1.4 to 1.6 and keep lines to 50 to 80 characters (see line-length); adjust by eye for the typeface's x-height.
Tighten the ratio for large headings (about 1.0 to 1.3), because the absolute gap grows with size.
When the layout widens the line, do not reduce the ratio; raise it slightly if lines exceed about 75 characters. This is convention.
Use unitless line-height values so that the ratio follows the font size.
antiPatterns: A line height computed from the golden ratio and presented as optimal.
One fixed pixel line height applied to every text size.
Body text at a ratio of 1.2 on lines of 100 characters.

howToCheck.machine: For each text style compute ratio = computed line height / computed font size. Body text: warn outside 1.4 to 1.6 and fail below the Prescription floor (WCAG 1.4.8 at level AAA asks for at least 1.5 within paragraphs). Headings above 32 px: warn outside 1.0 to 1.3. Compute characters per line = characters in a paragraph / rendered line count, at each breakpoint; flag any breakpoint where characters per line rises by more than 20% while the ratio falls. No validated formula links the three values, so the tool should check ranges and direction, not an 'ideal' value.
howToCheck.human: Read three paragraphs at the widest layout. If the eye lands on the wrong line, raise the ratio or narrow the column.

evidence.strengthNote: Search summaries of secondary sources only. Tinker's 1963 book Legibility of Print summarises studies from 1927 to 1959; a secondary page gives the 10-point safety zone of 14 to 31 picas and the 19-pica, 2-point combination, and warns that the methods look questionable; a typography blog that cites the book says 2 points of extra space performed best at each line width tested. Luckiesh and Moss reportedly found the opposite trend for line width. A practitioner series on optimal line height calls the golden-ratio formula 'a conclusion without proof'. The 1.4 to 1.6 body range and the heading range are convention reported by practitioner articles. The WCAG 1.5 value was read for the existing record spacing-and-justification, not again here. No experiment on line height as a function of line length for screen text was found.

sources.citation: Tinker, M. A. (1963). Legibility of Print. Iowa State University Press. (Seen through a secondary summary of its safety-zone table.)
Microsoft Typography blog (archived). More on linespacing (cites Tinker on 2 points of line spacing).
Kudamatsu, M. Optimal line-height reconsidered, parts 1 to 3 (practitioner series; argues for x-height and characters per line as the basis and criticises the golden-ratio formula).
W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.8 Visual Presentation, Level AAA (line spacing at least space-and-a-half).

entries.caveats: Print results for 10-point type on paper do not transfer directly to screens, different typefaces and different reading distances. Typefaces with a large x-height need more line spacing than the ratio suggests. Languages with tall accents or non-Latin scripts need more room. The existing records line-length and spacing-and-justification hold the reading evidence; this record covers the claimed formulas.

entries.principle: Fractal dimension: a mid-range preference for patterns in some studies; untested for interfaces
entries.claim: A fractal pattern repeats similar detail at many scales, and its fractal dimension D (between 1 and 2 for a flat pattern) says how densely it fills the plane. One line of studies found that people prefer patterns with D of about 1.3 to 1.5, the range common in natural scenes. Later studies found that preference rises steadily with D for some pattern types and that people differ. No study found applies fractal dimension to web pages or interfaces.
entries.mechanism: D is measured by box counting: cover the pattern with a grid of boxes of side e, count the boxes N(e) that contain part of the pattern, repeat for smaller e, and take D = the slope of log N(e) plotted against log(1 / e). A smooth line gives 1; a pattern that fills the area gives 2. The proposed explanation for a mid-range preference is that the visual system is tuned to the statistics of natural scenes, which fall in that range, so such patterns are processed easily. An interface is mostly text, boxes and photographs arranged by rules; it is not a self-similar pattern, so its box-counting number mostly reflects how much text and how many edges it has, which complexity measures capture more directly.

effects.cognitiveLoad: unknown — not measured for interfaces
effects.satisfaction: unknown — for interfaces; for abstract and natural patterns, mid-range D was preferred on average in some studies

designMoves: Do not tune a layout toward a fractal dimension.
If the design uses a decorative texture or background pattern, prefer natural-looking, mid-density patterns over very sparse or very dense ones, and keep them behind content with ample contrast.
Use compressed file size or edge density to measure the complexity of a page (see complexity-measures-and-preference-curve).
antiPatterns: Claiming that a page is 'naturally pleasing' because its fractal dimension is 1.4.
Dense fractal or noise textures behind text.
Treating the 1.3 to 1.5 range as universal.

howToCheck.machine: No validated check exists for interfaces. For a decorative background image or texture only, a program can compute D by box counting on the image's edge map (count occupied boxes at sides of 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 pixels; fit the slope of log count against log(1 / side)) and report it, with 1.3 to 1.5 as the range that some pattern studies favour. Do not fail a build on it and do not compute it for whole pages.
howToCheck.human: Ask whether the texture distracts from the text placed over it.

evidence.strengthNote: Grade B describes the pattern studies; for use on interfaces the grade is D, because one targeted search found no study. All sources were seen as search summaries. Spehar, Clifford, Newell and Taylor (2003), as later papers report it: low preference below about 1.2 and above about 1.6, highest at 1.3 to 1.5, for natural, mathematical and painted fractals. Bies and colleagues (2016): for exact (strictly repeating) fractals, preference rose with D for most participants, and symmetry and depth of repetition mattered. Street and colleagues (2016): 443 participants from several countries; mid-range patterns showed the most consistent preference, with individual differences in liking for complexity. Forsythe and colleagues (2011): fractal dimension added to the prediction of beauty in art, but compressed file size predicted more, and fractal dimension alone could not account for beauty judgments.

sources.citation: Spehar, B., Clifford, C. W. G., Newell, B. R., & Taylor, R. P. (2003). Universal aesthetic of fractals. Computers & Graphics, 27(5), 813-820. (Seen as reported by later papers; volume and pages recalled from memory.)

Bies, A. J., Blanc-Goldhammer, D. R., Boydston, C. R., Taylor, R. P., & Sereno, M. E. (2016). Aesthetic responses to exact fractals driven by physical complexity. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 10, 210. (Author list recalled from memory.)

Street, N., Forsythe, A. M., Reilly, R., Taylor, R., & Helmy, M. S. (2016). A complex story: Universal preference vs. individual differences shaping aesthetic response to fractals patterns. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience, 10, 213. (Author list recalled from memory.)
Forsythe, A., Nadal, M., Sheehy, N., Cela-Conde, C. J., & Sawey, M. (2011). Predicting beauty: Fractal dimension and visual complexity in art. British Journal of Psychology, 102(1), 49-70.

entries.caveats: Box-counting results depend on image size, the edge detector and the range of box sizes, so numbers from different tools do not compare. Studies of installed fractal floor and wall patterns exist for buildings; they concern physical spaces, not screens. The mid-range result may reflect an average over people who prefer different levels.
